21.translation: He states rajasic knowledge with ‘by separateness.’ ‘The knowledge which knows by separateness’ is itself explained: in all beings, in bodies, it knows many realities—many knowers of the field actually distinct, of separate kinds, differentiated as happy, unhappy, and so forth. Know that knowledge as rajasic.
word_for_word: rājasaṃ jñānam āha — pṛthaktvena iti
he states rajasic knowledge with ‘by separateness’
pṛthaktvena tu yat jñānam iti asya eva vivaraṇam
‘the knowledge which knows by separateness’ is itself explained
sarveṣu bhūteṣu deheṣu nānā-bhāvān vastuta eva anekān kṣetrajñān
in all beings, in bodies, it knows many realities—many knowers of the field actually distinct
pṛthag-vidhān sukhī duḥkhī ity-ādi-rūpeṇa vilakṣaṇān
of separate kinds, differentiated as happy, unhappy, and so forth
yena jñānena vetti tat jñānaṃ rājasaṃ viddhi
know that knowledge as rajasic

22.translation: He states tamasic knowledge with ‘but that which.’ Attached to one effect, a body or an image and so forth, as though it were the whole, as though complete—possessed of the insistence, ‘the Self is only this much’ or ‘the Lord is only this much’; causeless, without rational ground; having an object that is not the truth, empty of reliance on the ultimate reality; therefore also small, trivial, because its object is small and its fruit is small. Knowledge of such a kind is declared tamasic.
word_for_word: tāmasaṃ jñānam āha — yat tu iti
he states tamasic knowledge with ‘but that which’
ekasmin kārye dehe pratimā-ādau vā kṛtsnavat paripūrṇavat saktam
attached to one effect, a body or an image and so forth, as though it were the whole, as though complete
etāvān eva ātmā īśvaro vā iti abhiniveśa-yuktam
possessed of the insistence, ‘the Self is only this much’ or ‘the Lord is only this much’
ahaitukaṃ nirupapattikam
causeless, without rational ground
atattvārthavat paramārtha-avalambana-śūnyam
having an object that is not the truth, empty of reliance on the ultimate reality
ata eva alpaṃ tuccham
therefore also small, trivial
alpa-viṣayatvāt alpa-phalatvāt ca
because its object is small and its fruit is small
yat evaṃ-bhūtaṃ jñānaṃ tat tāmasam udāhṛtam
knowledge of such a kind is declared tamasic

23.translation: Now he states threefold action in the three verses beginning ‘prescribed.’ Prescribed: enjoined as obligatory. Free from attachment: devoid of insistence. Not done from attraction or aversion—either through affection for a son and so forth or through hatred of an enemy. Done by a doer who is without desire, the opposite of one who seeks fruit, one who wishes to obtain a result. The action so done is called sattvic.
word_for_word: idānīṃ trividhaṃ karma āha — niyatam iti tribhiḥ
now he states threefold action in the three verses beginning ‘prescribed’
niyataṃ nityatayā vihitam
prescribed: enjoined as obligatory
saṅga-rahitam abhiniveśa-śūnyam
free from attachment: devoid of insistence
arāga-dveṣataḥ
not from attraction or aversion
putra-ādi-prītyā vā śatru-dveṣeṇa vā yat kṛtaṃ na bhavati
not done either through affection for a son and so forth or through hatred of an enemy
phalaṃ prāptum icchati iti phala-prepsuḥ
one who wishes to obtain a result is a seeker of fruit
tad-vilakṣaṇena niṣkāmeṇa kartrā yat kṛtaṃ karma
action done by a desireless doer, the opposite of that
tat sāttvikam ucyate
that is called sattvic

24.translation: He states rajasic action with ‘but that which.’ Action performed by one desiring, wishing to obtain the fruit; or by one with ego, firmly possessed of the conceit ‘what other learned Vedic scholar is equal to me?’; and again, action accompanied by much exertion, excessive strain—that action is declared rajasic.
word_for_word: rājasaṃ karma āha — yat tu iti
he states rajasic action with ‘but that which’
yat tu karma kāma-īpsunā phalaṃ prāptum icchatā
action performed by one desiring, wishing to obtain the fruit
sāhaṅkāreṇa vā matsamaḥ ko anyaḥ śrotriyaḥ asti iti evaṃ nirūḍha-ahaṅkāra-yuktena ca kriyate
or by one with ego, firmly possessed of the conceit ‘what other learned Vedic scholar is equal to me?’
yat ca punaḥ bahula-āyāsam ati-kleśa-yuktam
and again, action accompanied by much exertion, excessive strain
tat karma rājasam udāhṛtam
that action is declared rajasic

25.translation: He states tamasic action with ‘consequence.’ Consequence means the good or bad that will follow later. Loss means expenditure of wealth. Violence means causing pain to another. Prowess means one’s own capacity. Action that is begun merely from delusion, without considering, without examining, these things is called tamasic.
word_for_word: tāmasaṃ karma āha — anubandham iti
he states tamasic action with ‘consequence’
anubadhyate iti anubandhaḥ paścāt-bhāvi śubha-aśubham
consequence means the good or bad that will follow later
kṣayaṃ vitta-vyayam
loss means expenditure of wealth
hiṃsāṃ para-pīḍāṃ ca
violence means causing pain to another
pauruṣaṃ sva-sāmarthyaṃ vā
prowess means one’s own capacity
anavekṣya aparyālocya
without considering, without examining
kevalaṃ mohāt eva yat karma ārabhyate
action that is begun merely from delusion
tat tāmasam ucyate
that is called tamasic

26.translation: He states the doer as threefold in the three verses beginning ‘free from attachment.’ Free from attachment means having abandoned insistence. Not speaking ‘I’ means devoid of boastful speech. Fortitude is courage; enthusiasm is exertion; endowed means joined with those two. Unchanged in the success or failure of an undertaken action means free from joy and dejection. A doer of such a kind is called sattvic.
word_for_word: kartāraṃ trividham āha — mukta-saṅga iti tribhiḥ
he states the doer as threefold in the three verses beginning ‘free from attachment’
mukta-saṅgaḥ tyakta-abhiniveśaḥ
free from attachment means having abandoned insistence
anahaṃ-vādī garva-ukti-rahitaḥ
not speaking ‘I’ means devoid of boastful speech
dhṛtiḥ dhairyam
fortitude is courage
utsāhaḥ udyamaḥ
enthusiasm is exertion
tābhyāṃ samanvitaḥ saṃyuktaḥ
endowed means joined with those two
ārabdhasya karmaṇaḥ siddhau asiddhau ca nirvikāraḥ harṣa-viṣāda-śūnyaḥ
unchanged in the success or failure of an undertaken action means free from joy and dejection
evaṃ-bhūtaḥ kartā sāttvika ucyate
a doer of such a kind is called sattvic

27.translation: He states the rajasic doer with ‘attached.’ Attached means possessing affection for a son and so forth. A seeker of the fruit of action means desiring the fruit of action. Greedy means desiring another’s property. Violent by nature means having a killing disposition. Impure means lacking the prescribed purity. Endowed with joy and sorrow at gain and loss: such a doer is declared rajasic.
word_for_word: rājasaṃ kartāram āha — rāgī iti
he states the rajasic doer with ‘attached’
rāgī putra-ādi-prītimān
attached means possessing affection for a son and so forth
karma-phala-prepsuḥ karma-phala-kāmī
a seeker of the fruit of action means desiring the fruit of action
lubdhaḥ para-sva-abhilāṣī
greedy means desiring another’s property
hiṃsātmakaḥ māraka-svabhāvaḥ
violent by nature means having a killing disposition
aśuciḥ vihita-śauca-śūnyaḥ
impure means lacking the prescribed purity
lābha-alābhayoḥ harṣa-śokābhyām anvitaḥ
endowed with joy and sorrow at gain and loss
kartā rājasaḥ parikīrtitaḥ
such a doer is declared rajasic

28.translation: He states the tamasic doer with ‘unintegrated.’ Unintegrated means inattentive. Prākṛta means devoid of discrimination. Stiff means not humble. Deceitful means one who conceals his capacity. Naiṣkṛtika means one who insults others. Lazy means of a nature without exertion. Despondent means habitually sorrowful. One who does not complete even in a month a task that should be done today or tomorrow is long-procrastinating. A doer of such a kind is called tamasic. By the threefoldness of the doer, the threefoldness of the knower also has been stated. By the threefoldness of action, the threefoldness of the knowable also should be understood as stated. By the threefoldness of the intellect, the threefoldness of the instrument also will have been stated.
word_for_word: tāmasaṃ kartāram āha — ayukta iti
he states the tamasic doer with ‘unintegrated’
ayuktaḥ anavahitaḥ
unintegrated means inattentive
prākṛtaḥ viveka-śūnyaḥ
prākṛta means devoid of discrimination
stabdhaḥ anamraḥ
stiff means not humble
śaṭhaḥ śakti-gūhana-kārī
deceitful means one who conceals his capacity
naiṣkṛtikaḥ para-avamānī
naiṣkṛtika means one who insults others
alasaḥ anudyama-śīlaḥ
lazy means of a nature without exertion
viṣādī śoka-śīlaḥ
despondent means habitually sorrowful
yat adya vā śvaḥ vā kāryaṃ tat māsena api na saṃpādayati yaḥ sa dīrgha-sūtrī
one who does not complete even in a month a task that should be done today or tomorrow is long-procrastinating
evaṃ-bhūtaḥ kartā tāmasa ucyate
a doer of such a kind is called tamasic
kartṛ-traividhyena eva jñātuḥ api traividhyam uktaṃ bhavati
by the threefoldness of the doer, the threefoldness of the knower also has been stated
karma-traividhyena ca jñeyasya api traividhyam uktaṃ veditavyam
by the threefoldness of action, the threefoldness of the knowable also should be understood as stated
buddheḥ traividhyena karaṇasya api traividhyam uktaṃ bhaviṣyati
by the threefoldness of the intellect, the threefoldness of the instrument also will have been stated

29.translation: Now he promises the threefoldness of the intellect and also of fortitude with ‘the intellect.’ The meaning is clear.
word_for_word: idānīṃ buddheḥ dhṛteḥ ca api traividhyaṃ pratijānīte — buddhiḥ iti
now he promises the threefoldness of the intellect and also of fortitude with ‘the intellect’
spaṣṭa-arthaḥ
the meaning is clear

30.translation: There he states the threefoldness of the intellect in the three verses beginning ‘activity and.’ Activity in dharma and withdrawal from adharma; what is to be done and not to be done in a given place and time; fear and fearlessness, namely benefit and harm caused by what is to be done and not done; how bondage occurs and how liberation occurs—the intellect, the inner organ, that knows these is sattvic. Where one ought to say ‘by which a person knows,’ agency is figuratively attributed to the instrument, as in ‘the pieces of wood cook.’
word_for_word: tatra buddheḥ traividhyam āha — pravṛttiṃ ca iti tribhiḥ
there he states the threefoldness of the intellect in the three verses beginning ‘activity and’
pravṛttiṃ ca dharme nivṛttiṃ ca adharme
activity in dharma and withdrawal from adharma
yasmin deśe kāle ca yat kāryam akāryaṃ ca
what is to be done and not to be done in a given place and time
bhaya-abhaye kārya-akārya-nimittau artha-anarthau
fear and fearlessness, namely benefit and harm caused by what is to be done and not done
kathaṃ bandhaḥ kathaṃ vā mokṣaḥ iti
how bondage occurs and how liberation occurs
yā buddhiḥ antaḥkaraṇaṃ vetti sā sāttvikī
the intellect, the inner organ, that knows these is sattvic
yayā pumān vetti iti vaktavye karaṇe kartṛtva-upacāraḥ
where one ought to say ‘by which a person knows,’ agency is figuratively attributed to the instrument
kāṣṭhāni pacanti iti vat
as in ‘the pieces of wood cook’

31.translation: He states the rajasic intellect with ‘by which.’ ‘Not as it really is’ means as a matter open to doubt. The rest is clear.
word_for_word: rājasīṃ buddhim āha — yayā iti
he states the rajasic intellect with ‘by which’
ayathāvat saṃdeha-āspadatvena iti arthaḥ
‘not as it really is’ means as a matter open to doubt
spaṣṭam anyat
the rest is clear

32.translation: He states the tamasic intellect with ‘adharma.’ The meaning is: an intellect that grasps the opposite is tamasic. Intellect as the inner organ was stated earlier. Knowledge is its modification. Fortitude too is a modification of it. Or, even intellect, as a property of the inner organ that is the possessor of properties, is itself a modification characterized by ascertainment. Although its modifications such as desire and aversion are many, the threefoldness of these is stated because they are principal as means of dharma and adharma, fear and fearlessness. And this is an indicative example for the others.
word_for_word: tāmasīṃ buddhim āha — adharmam iti
he states the tamasic intellect with ‘adharma’
viparīta-grāhiṇī buddhiḥ tāmasī iti arthaḥ
an intellect that grasps the opposite is tamasic: this is the meaning
buddhiḥ antaḥkaraṇaṃ pūrvoktam
intellect as the inner organ was stated earlier
jñānaṃ tu tad-vṛttiḥ
knowledge is its modification
dhṛtiḥ api tad-vṛttiḥ eva
fortitude too is a modification of it
yad vā antaḥkaraṇasya dharmiṇaḥ buddhiḥ api adhyavasāya-lakṣaṇāt vṛttiḥ eva
or even intellect, as a property of the inner organ that is the possessor of properties, is itself a modification characterized by ascertainment
icchā-dveṣa-ādīnāṃ tad-vṛttīnāṃ bahutve api
although its modifications such as desire and aversion are many
dharma-adharma-bhaya-abhaya-sādhanatvena prādhānyāt etāsāṃ traividhyam uktam
the threefoldness of these is stated because they are principal as means of dharma and adharma, fear and fearlessness
upalakṣaṇaṃ ca etad anyāsām
and this is an indicative example for the others

33.translation: Now he states the threefoldness of fortitude in the three verses beginning ‘by fortitude.’ The fortitude by which, through yoga—concentration of mind—as its cause, unwaveringly, not supporting another object, one holds, restrains, the activities of mind, vital breath, and senses: that fortitude is sattvic.
word_for_word: idānīṃ dhṛteḥ traividhyam āha — dhṛtyā iti tribhiḥ
now he states the threefoldness of fortitude in the three verses beginning ‘by fortitude’
yogena citta-ekāgryeṇa hetunā
through yoga—concentration of mind—as its cause
avyabhicāriṇyā viṣaya-antaram adhārayantyā yayā dhṛtyā
by the fortitude that is unwavering, not supporting another object
manasaḥ prāṇasya indriyāṇāṃ ca kriyā dhārayate niyacchati
one holds, restrains, the activities of mind, vital breath, and senses
sā dhṛtiḥ sāttvikī
that fortitude is sattvic

34.translation: He states rajasic fortitude with ‘but by which.’ The fortitude by which one chiefly holds fast to dharma, wealth, and desire and does not release them, and through attachment to them becomes desirous of their fruit, is rajasic fortitude.
word_for_word: rājasīṃ dhṛtim āha — yayā tu iti
he states rajasic fortitude with ‘but by which’
yayā tu dhṛtyā dharma-artha-kāmān prādhānyena dhārayate
the fortitude by which one chiefly holds fast to dharma, wealth, and desire
na vimuñcati
does not release them
tat-prasaṅgena phala-ākāṅkṣī ca bhavati
and through attachment to them becomes desirous of their fruit
sā rājasī dhṛtiḥ
that is rajasic fortitude

35.translation: He states tamasic fortitude with ‘by which.’ A person whose intelligence is bad, full of non-discrimination, is ‘of bad intelligence.’ The fortitude by which such a person does not release sleep and the others, but repeatedly returns to them—‘dream’ here means sleep—that fortitude is tamasic.
word_for_word: tāmasīṃ dhṛtim āha — yayā iti
he states tamasic fortitude with ‘by which’
duṣṭā aviveka-bahulā medhā yasya sa durmedhāḥ puruṣaḥ
a person whose intelligence is bad, full of non-discrimination, is ‘of bad intelligence’
yayā dhṛtyā svapna-ādīn na vimuñcati punaḥ punaḥ āvartayati
the fortitude by which such a person does not release sleep and the others, but repeatedly returns to them
svapnaḥ atra nidrā
‘dream’ here means sleep
sā dhṛtiḥ tāmasī
that fortitude is tamasic

36.translation: With half a verse he promises the threefoldness of happiness with ‘happiness.’ The meaning is clear. There, with a verse and a half beginning ‘from practice,’ he states sattvic happiness: the happiness in which one delights through practice, through very great familiarity, but does not obtain delight suddenly as in sensory pleasure; and, delighting in which, one thoroughly reaches, attains, the end, the cessation, of suffering.
word_for_word: sukhasya traividhyaṃ pratijānīte ardhena — sukham iti
with half a verse he promises the threefoldness of happiness with ‘happiness’
spaṣṭa-arthaḥ
the meaning is clear
tatra sāttvikaṃ sukham āha — abhyāsāt iti sārdhena
there, with a verse and a half beginning ‘from practice,’ he states sattvic happiness
yatra yasmin sukhe abhyāsāt ati-paricayāt ramate
the happiness in which one delights through practice, through very great familiarity
na tu viṣaya-sukhe iva sahasā ratiṃ prāpnoti
but does not obtain delight suddenly as in sensory pleasure
yasmin ramamāṇaḥ ca duḥkhasya antam avasānaṃ nitarāṃ gacchati prāpnoti
and delighting in which, one thoroughly reaches, attains, the end, the cessation, of suffering

37.translation: What is that like? He says ‘that which.’ Whatever that happiness is, at first it is like poison, as if producing pain because it depends on restraint of the mind; but in the result it is like nectar. The intellect concerning the Self is ‘self-intellect.’ Through its clarity—remaining clear after abandoning the impurities rajas and tamas—the happiness born from that is called sattvic by yogins.
word_for_word: kīdṛśaṃ tat — yat tat iti
what is that like? he says ‘that which’
yat tat kim api agre prathamaṃ viṣam iva
whatever that happiness is, at first it is like poison
manaḥ-saṃyama-adhīnatvāt duḥkha-āvaham iva bhavati
as if producing pain because it depends on restraint of the mind
pariṇāme tu amṛta-sadṛśam
but in the result it is like nectar
ātma-viṣayā buddhiḥ ātma-buddhiḥ
the intellect concerning the Self is ‘self-intellect’
tasyāḥ prasādena rajas-tamo-mala-tyāgena svacchatayā avasthānam
through its clarity—remaining clear after abandoning the impurities rajas and tamas
tataḥ jātaṃ yat sukhaṃ tat sāttvikaṃ proktaṃ yogibhiḥ
the happiness born from that is called sattvic by yogins

38.translation: He states rajasic happiness with ‘object and sense.’ The well-known happiness, such as sexual union, arising from contact between sense objects and the senses, is at first of such a kind that nectar is its simile. But in the result it is equal to poison, because here and hereafter it causes suffering. That happiness is remembered as rajasic.
word_for_word: rājasaṃ sukham āha — viṣaya-indriya iti
he states rajasic happiness with ‘object and sense’
viṣayāṇām indriyāṇāṃ ca saṃyogāt yat tat prasiddhaṃ strī-saṅga-ādi sukham
the well-known happiness, such as sexual union, arising from contact between sense objects and the senses
amṛtam upamā yasya tādṛśaṃ bhavati agre prathamam
is at first of such a kind that nectar is its simile
pariṇāme tu viṣa-tulyam
but in the result it is equal to poison
iha amutra ca duḥkha-hetutvāt
because here and hereafter it causes suffering
tat sukhaṃ rājasaṃ smṛtam
that happiness is remembered as rajasic

39.translation: He states tamasic happiness with ‘which.’ The happiness that deludes the self at first, in the first moment, and in its consequence, afterward as well. He states it specifically: sleep, laziness, and negligence; the happiness that arises from these, namely mental wandering through lack of attention to what ought to be done, is declared tamasic.
word_for_word: tāmasaṃ sukham āha — yat iti
he states tamasic happiness with ‘which’
agre prathama-kṣaṇe anubandhe ca paścāt api yat sukham ātmanaḥ moha-karam
the happiness that deludes the self at first, in the first moment, and in its consequence, afterward as well
tat eva āha
he states it specifically
nidrā ca ālasyaṃ ca pramādaḥ ca
sleep, laziness, and negligence
kartavya-artha-avadhāna-rāhityena manorājyam
mental wandering through lack of attention to what ought to be done
etebhyaḥ uttiṣṭhati yat sukhaṃ tat tāmasam udāhṛtam
the happiness that arises from these is declared tamasic

40.translation: Gathering up even what has not been stated, he concludes the subject with ‘there is not that.’ There is nowhere on earth, in the human worlds and so forth, or in heaven among the gods, any being—any living species or anything else—that is free, devoid, of these three guṇas beginning with sattva, which arise from prakṛti. This is the meaning.
word_for_word: anuktam api saṃgṛhṇan prakaraṇa-artham upasaṃharati — na tad asti iti
gathering up even what has not been stated, he concludes the subject with ‘there is not that’
ebhiḥ prakṛti-saṃbhavaiḥ sattva-ādibhiḥ tribhiḥ guṇaiḥ muktaṃ hīnaṃ sattvam
any being free, devoid, of these three guṇas beginning with sattva, which arise from prakṛti
prāṇi-jātam anyad vā yat syāt
any living species or anything else
tat pṛthivyāṃ manuṣya-loka-ādiṣu divi deveṣu ca kva api na asti
there is nowhere on earth, in the human worlds and so forth, or in heaven among the gods
iti arthaḥ
this is the meaning
